design_detail: Special article in World Psychiatry (2016;15(3):195–204), read in full in PubMed Central, by five authors from the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, King's College London. A narrative review arguing that cannabis use, and especially use of high-potency cannabis and synthetic cannabinoids, increases the risk of psychosis, with shorter sections on other psychiatric disorders, brain and cognition, adolescent vulnerability and therapeutic uses. No search strategy, selection criteria, appraisal or pooling; 166 references; one table listing 13 adjusted odds ratios from 12 longitudinal studies without their exposure, outcome or adjustment definitions.
can_establish: The case for a causal, dose-related and potency-related effect of cannabis on psychosis as argued in 2016 by a research group that produced much of the potency evidence, its answers to the main criticisms (prior vulnerability, self-medication, other drugs, incidence trends, shared genetic liability), and pointers to the primary studies on each.
cannot_establish: Whether, or how much, cannabis causes psychosis (no systematic search or appraisal; the potency and cannabidiol evidence comes largely from the authors' group; the table's estimates lack exposure, outcome and adjustment definitions), the relative risk of high-potency products or synthetic cannabinoids beyond the few studies cited, or effects on cognition, which the body itself describes as mixed.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence was chosen by the authors; no databases, dates or criteria are given.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The cohorts in Table 1 are from the USA, Sweden, the Netherlands, Israel, New Zealand, Germany, the UK and Switzerland; the potency evidence comes mainly from first-episode samples in south London; the cognition evidence from New Zealand, the UK, the USA and Australia.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors'. 13 of the 166 references list one of the review's authors among their printed names (editors' count; lists cut to three names and et al. may hide more): the potency case–control and age-at-onset studies (refs 66–68), the dose–response meta-analysis (ref 65), the AKT1 replication (ref 95), the cannabidiol experiment (ref 35), a THC-paranoia experiment (ref 26), a COMT experiment (ref 93), a corpus callosum imaging study (ref 136), an earlier review (ref 14) and three commentaries or replies (refs 51, 90, 101). The claims that go beyond the cohort association (potency, cannabidiol, gene–environment interaction) rest largely on these. Critics are represented by four North American articles (refs 80–82, 86), named and answered.

exposure.measurement: Not stated in Table 1. Definitions used in the text include use more than 50 times by conscription (Andréasson et al.), daily or weekly use, high-potency (skunk-like) cannabis against hashish, cannabidiol content judged by preference or hair analysis, cannabis use disorder diagnosed at several assessments (the Dunedin IQ analysis), age at onset (15 or younger, before 17, 18 or older) and synthetic cannabinoids.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Potency, as cited: THC 3% or less in herbal cannabis and resin in the 1960s; averages of 16% in England and 20% in the Netherlands in the early 2000s, with high-potency sinsemilla displacing resin and containing only traces of cannabidiol (refs 37, 38); about 15% in Australia (ref 39); a US average of 12% by 2014 (ref 40); resin oil of up to 80% THC (no citation). Onset and duration by route are stated without a citation (CANNABINOIDS AND THE ENDOCANNABINOID SYSTEM, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Treated as one criticism of the causal hypothesis: the review says studies that addressed other drug use, including tobacco, did not find it sufficient to negate the effect of cannabis (refs 58, 66, 67); other drug use in the remaining studies is not described.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not stated for the cited cognitive studies; recovery after stopping is described as full in some studies (ref 144) and partial in others (ref 142).

comparison.controls: People who never used cannabis (most cited estimates); healthy controls recruited for the south London first-episode study; patients with psychosis who never used cannabis (age at onset, IQ, neurological soft signs); placebo or pre-treatment conditions in the cannabidiol experiments.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review argues that prior vulnerability does not explain the association, citing adjustment for psychotic symptoms at age 11 in the Dunedin cohort (ref 58) and the better premorbid IQ and social functioning of patients who used cannabis (refs 76–79). It leaves open how far genetic predisposition is correlated with, or interacts with, use, and concedes uncertainty about whether cannabis can induce psychosis without genetic vulnerability (GENETIC PREDISPOSITION OR GENE X ENVIRONMENT INTERACTION?; CONCLUSIONS, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed for the cited studies.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: psychotic symptoms or experiences (population cohorts and surveys), psychotic disorder at first episode (case–control), schizophrenia diagnoses (Swedish conscript registers), age at onset of psychosis, relapse and admission; IQ and neuropsychological tests; MRI measures; dependence; depression, anxiety, PTSD and ADHD; educational attainment.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis spans self-reported psychotic symptoms to diagnosed schizophrenia; Table 1 does not say which outcome, exposure contrast or adjustment each odds ratio refers to, although its header calls the estimates adjusted.

analysis.effect_sizes: All second-hand; no pooling. Table 1, adjusted odds ratios for psychotic outcomes: Tien & Anthony 2.4 (1.2–7.1); Zammit et al. 3.1 (1.7–5.5); Manrique-Garcia et al. 1.8 (1.3–2.3); van Os et al. 2.8 (1.2–6.5); Weiser et al. 2.0 (1.3–3.1); Fergusson et al. 1.8 (1.2–2.6); Arseneault et al. 4.5 (1.1–18.2); Ferdinand et al. 2.8 (1.79–4.43); Henquet et al. 1.7 (printed interval 1.1–1.5); Wiles et al. 1.5 (0.55–3.94); Rössler et al. 1.8 (0.96–3.2); Gage et al. 1.1 (0.76–1.65); Rognli et al. 2.6 (1.40–5.0). Andréasson et al.: use more than 50 times, six times the risk of schizophrenia over 15 years. Marconi et al.: odds ratio of almost 4 for the heaviest use against none. Di Forti et al. (2015): daily high-potency use, five times the odds of psychotic disorder; Di Forti et al. (2014): first episode on average 6 years earlier with daily high-potency use than with no use; proportion of psychosis preventable 8–24% (ref 66). Synthetic cannabinoids: 30 times more likely to need emergency treatment than plant cannabis in a survey of 80,000 people who use drugs (ref 45). Dependence: almost 10% of people who use (refs 105, 106), 17% with adolescent onset (ref 107). Cognition: a fall of six IQ points between ages 13 and 38 in Dunedin members repeatedly diagnosed with cannabis use disorder (ref 139); in CARDIA, 5,115 people over 25 years, worse verbal memory but not executive function or processing speed (ref 142). Pain: number needed to treat 5.6 for inhaled cannabis in chronic neuropathic pain (ref 155).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable; the adjustment sets behind Table 1 are not given.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection in support of the causal hypothesis. The critics' arguments are summarized and answered, but the evidence they rely on is not described: no study reporting stable schizophrenia incidence is cited; the reverse direction in a cohort listed in Table 1, whose title reports that psychotic symptoms also predict cannabis use (Ferdinand et al., 2005), is not discussed; and the finding that genetic liability to schizophrenia predicts cannabis use (Power et al., 2014) is reported only as accounting for a very small proportion of use.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Most prospective cohorts in Table 1 report adjusted odds ratios of about 1.5 to 4.5 for psychotic outcomes, and three are non-significant; a meta-analysis from the authors' group reports an odds ratio of almost 4 for the heaviest use. In one south London case–control study, daily use of high-potency cannabis went with about five times the odds of psychotic disorder, and hashish with no increase. Intravenous THC produces transient psychotic symptoms, and in one experiment oral cannabidiol given beforehand reduced them. Evidence on depression, anxiety, PTSD and ADHD is weak; the cognitive findings are mixed (the Dunedin decline, two failures to replicate it, full or partial recovery after stopping).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract names high-potency cannabis and synthetic cannabinoids as the riskiest forms, a claim that rests on one group's case–control and onset studies of potency (refs 66–68), case reports and a systematic overview of psychopathology after synthetic cannabinoids. It says there are "no such doubts concerning its detrimental effect on cognitive function" (Abstract), while the body reports two failures to replicate the Dunedin IQ decline, full recovery after stopping in some studies, and small, poorly controlled imaging studies. It says all of the negative aspects are magnified when use starts in early adolescence, while the body says the imaging reports await confirmation and that social decline was not associated with age at onset. The conclusion that the evidence for cannabis as a component cause of psychosis suffices for public-health messages is the authors' judgment, supported by a quotation from Gage et al. (2016); the body concedes uncertainty about causation without genetic vulnerability and about the preventable fraction (8–24%, cited to the authors' own study and presented as the share preventable if nobody used cannabis; the review does not say that such fractions assume causality). The statement that most European and Australasian experts are convinced of a contributory cause carries no citation.

timeline.event: Swedish conscript cohort (Andréasson et al., 1987), described here as 45,750 men, with six times the risk of schizophrenia over 15 years for use more than 50 times (adjustment not stated); Hall & Degenhardt (2009) give 50,465 men and 2.4 times for any use by 18 (card sc_hall_2009).

Dunedin cohort (Arseneault et al., 2002), cited as adjusting for psychotic symptoms at 11 and as showing a fourfold risk of schizophrenia-like psychosis by 26 with onset at 15 or younger; Table 1 gives 4.5 (1.1–18.2).
27-year follow-up of the Swedish conscripts (Zammit et al., 2002), Table 1: 3.1 (1.7–5.5) in 50,053; 35-year follow-up (Manrique-Garcia et al., 2012): 1.8 (1.3–2.3).

Dunedin COMT gene–environment report (Caspi et al., 2005); the review says attempted replications have been inconsistent and cites an experiment finding no COMT effect on THC-induced psychotic symptoms (Tunbridge et al., 2015).
Dutch cohort whose title reports that cannabis use predicts psychotic symptoms and vice versa (Ferdinand et al., 2005), listed in Table 1 (2.8, 1.79–4.43); the reverse direction is not discussed.

South-east London study of first presentations with schizophrenia 1965–1999 (Boydell et al., 2006), cited as the only competent long-term incidence study: incidence doubled and cannabis use among patients rose disproportionately. No study of stable incidence is cited, although one was cited in earlier reviews (Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003, in card sc_hall_2009).
Systematic review cited for weak evidence that cannabis increases the risk of affective outcomes (card sc_moore_2007).

Authors' group: high-potency cannabis and psychosis (Di Forti et al., 2009); age at onset 6 years earlier with daily high-potency use (Di Forti et al., 2014); south London case–control study (Di Forti et al., 2015), described here as 410 patients and 390 controls with a fivefold risk for daily high-potency use (card sc_di_forti_2015: 410 patients and 370 controls analysed; adjusted odds ratio 5.40).
Polygenic risk for schizophrenia associated with cannabis use in Australians (Power et al., 2014), reported here only as explaining a very small proportion of use.

Letter suggesting that people using high-potency cannabis may be especially genetically predisposed (Gage et al., 2015) and the authors' correspondence reply, which this review cites as finding no evidence that people using high-potency cannabis were more genetically predisposed, judged by schizophrenia polygenic scores (Di Forti et al., 2015; no figures given here).
Christchurch cohort (Fergusson et al., 2015), cited against self-medication: people tended to use less once minor psychotic symptoms developed.
Sceptical North American articles named and answered: Hill (2015), Ksir & Hart (2016, critical overview; and a 2016 letter), Haney & Evins (2016).
Epidemiological review whose conclusion is quoted: the evidence warrants a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk of psychotic disorders (card sc_gage_2016).
Dose–response meta-analysis from the authors' group (Marconi et al., 2016), cited for an odds ratio of almost 4 for the heaviest use (card sc_marconi_2016: 3.90, 2.84 to 5.34, unadjusted data).

Cognition: the Dunedin IQ decline (Meier et al., 2012) is set against two failures to replicate (Mokrysz et al., 2016; Jackson et al., 2016) and the CARDIA finding of worse verbal memory only (Auer et al., 2016).

After this review: two-sample Mendelian randomization studies (Gage et al., 2017; Vaucher et al., 2018) and a genome-wide study with bidirectional Mendelian randomization finding stronger evidence from liability to schizophrenia to cannabis use than the reverse (Pasman et al., 2018; card sc_pasman_2018), the shared-liability question this review leaves open; all read in this round.

After this review: the authors' group extended the potency case–control design to 901 cases and 1237 controls in 11 catchment areas in Europe and Brazil (Di Forti et al., 2019; card sc_di_forti_2019).
After this review: viewpoint on genetically informed methods for testing whether the cannabis–schizophrenia association is causal (card sc_gillespie_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: A 2016 position review by the group whose studies carry its potency and cannabidiol claims. The cohort association and its dose–response were already reported by others (Moore et al., 2007) and pooled by the authors' group (Marconi et al., 2016); the potency claim was later extended by the same group to 11 sites in Europe and Brazil; Mendelian randomization after 2016 has given mixed evidence for an effect of cannabis on schizophrenia and stronger evidence for genetic liability to schizophrenia predicting cannabis use, the shared-liability explanation that this review discounts. Cite it for its arguments and pointers, labelled as the authors' position, and take every figure from the primary study.

funding.funder: No funding statement appears in the PMC full text.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the PMC full text.
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors are at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience, King's College London, as printed. Murray (first author) and Di Forti (last author) are authors of the potency case–control and onset studies, the dose–response meta-analysis and the replies that carry the review's distinctive claims, and Englund of the cannabidiol experiment it cites. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective population cohorts that measure the THC and cannabidiol content of the cannabis actually used (product testing or biomarkers) before psychosis onset, with polygenic scores and family history to test interaction and shared liability, analysed within families (siblings or twins); and independent replication of the potency–psychosis association by groups outside south London in markets with different products.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.

No appraisal of individual studies. Table 1 gives estimates without exposure, outcome or adjustment definitions and contains an interval that excludes its own estimate; a supportive study is called the only competent one without appraisal, and studies relied on by critics are not described.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The potency, cannabidiol, dose–response and AKT1 evidence and three of the replies to critics are from the authors' group (at least 13 of 166 references).

The conclusions name uncertainties, but several statements are uncited or speculative: expert consensus in Europe and Australasia; withdrawal described as minor because cannabis stays in the body for weeks; resin oil of up to 80% THC; the explanation that patients who used cannabis were initially clever and sociable; post-synaptic dopamine supersensitivity proposed from animal data.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a causal effect of cannabis on psychosis
domains.note: The evidence for shared liability and reverse causation is under-represented: no stable-incidence study is cited, the reverse direction in a Table 1 cohort is not discussed, the polygenic finding that liability to schizophrenia predicts cannabis use is minimized, and the critics' case is given in a paragraph each with the authors' reply.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated risk-of-bias instrument exists for narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used and the overall judgment follows the worst domains. The review is an explicit argument for one side of a contested question, by the group whose studies carry its distinctive claims, without a search or appraisal; it states its uncertainties in the conclusions, but its abstract goes beyond its body on cognition, adolescence and potency. Cite it for the authors' position and their replies to critics, labelled as such, and as a pointer to primary studies; take every figure from the primary study. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft and must say its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3).

key_findings.finding: Abstract conclusions: epidemiological evidence shows an association between cannabis use and psychotic outcomes with a dose–response relation; high-potency cannabis and synthetic cannabinoids are the riskiest forms; experimentally given THC brings on brief psychosis in healthy volunteers, an effect that cannabidiol, present in traditional hashish but largely absent from modern high-potency cannabis, can reduce; evidence that cannabis increases the risk of other psychiatric disorders is not convincing, but there are, in the authors' words, "no such doubts concerning its detrimental effect on cognitive function"; all negative aspects are magnified when use starts in early adolescence; and the evidence that cannabis is a component cause of psychosis suffices for public-health messages on the risk, above all for frequent use of strong cannabis and of synthetic cannabinoids.

Context: about 180 million people use cannabis worldwide (ref 2, UNODC World Drug Report 2015); at the time Uruguay had legalized sale, cultivation and distribution (2013), four US states had legalized recreational use and 25 more states and Canada allowed medical use; the authors expect consumption to increase.

Composition and time course: cannabis contains more than 100 cannabinoids, chiefly THC and cannabidiol (ref 4); in some countries such as the USA it is smoked on its own, and in much of Europe with tobacco. Smoked or inhaled, effects begin within minutes and last 2–3 hours; eaten, they can take 2 hours to appear and last up to 8 hours (no citation).
key_findings.locator: CANNABINOIDS AND THE ENDOCANNABINOID SYSTEM, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The time course is uncited; take onset and duration by route from pharmacokinetic studies (for example Huestis, 2007, read in this round).

key_findings.finding: Acute effects: THC is a partial CB1 agonist; given to healthy volunteers it impairs learning, attention and memory in a dose-related way (refs 17–22), which the authors link to a doubled risk of traffic accidents when driving under the influence (ref 23, Hall, 2015). A sufficiently high intravenous dose can bring on brief psychotic symptoms such as paranoia and hallucinations (refs 19, 24, 25), and THC increases paranoid thoughts in a virtual-reality setting (ref 26). Cannabidiol has little CB1 affinity but appears to block or reduce many THC effects: tachycardia (ref 31), anxiety (ref 32), perceptual effects (refs 33, 34) and memory effects (ref 35).
key_findings.locator: CANNABINOIDS AND THE ENDOCANNABINOID SYSTEM, 5th–7th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The doubled crash risk is third-hand, through Hall (2015) from the 2012 meta-analyses (card sc_hall_2015), which were later re-analysed with lower corrected estimates (card sc_rogeberg_2016).

key_findings.finding: Potency, as cited: THC in herbal cannabis and resin was 3% or less in the 1960s and then rose; high-potency sinsemilla (skunk), bred for THC, contains only traces of cannabidiol (refs 36, 37). Average THC reached 16% in England and 20% in the Netherlands in the early 2000s, with sinsemilla displacing resin (refs 37, 38), about 15% in Australia (ref 39) and an average of 12% in the USA by 2014 (ref 40). In US states with legal markets, oils and edibles are increasingly available, extracts of up to 80% THC have appeared, and vaping and wax dabbing deliver high concentrations (no citation).
key_findings.locator: THE CHANGING NATURE OF RECREATIONAL CANNABINOIDS, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Synthetic cannabinoids: compounds synthesized over decades in a search for therapeutic cannabinoids (ref 41) came into use as legal highs from the late 2000s; unlike THC, a partial agonist with weak CB1 affinity, they are full agonists with generally higher affinity and pose a greater health risk (refs 42–44). In a survey of 80,000 people who use drugs, those who used synthetic cannabinoids were 30 times more likely to end up needing emergency treatment than those who used traditional cannabis (ref 45, Winstock et al., 2015). Reported acute physical effects are nausea and vomiting, shortness of breath, raised blood pressure, fast heart rate, chest pain and, occasionally, acute kidney failure; more than 200 compounds have been reported (ref 46), each with potentially unpredictable effects, and routine drug tests do not detect them.
key_findings.locator: THE CHANGING NATURE OF RECREATIONAL CANNABINOIDS, 4th–5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The 30-fold figure is second-hand from one survey; its design and denominators are not described here.

key_findings.finding: History: in 1896 a Scottish psychiatrist noted that 40 of 253 patients in the Cairo asylum had insanity attributed to hashish (ref 47). In the first prospective study, of 45,750 Swedish conscripts, those who had used cannabis more than 50 times were six times as likely to develop schizophrenia over the next 15 years as those who had never used it (ref 48, Andréasson et al., 1987); the authors say the finding was mostly ignored and that a 1995 Lancet editorial still held that even long-term smoking was not harmful to health (ref 49).
key_findings.note: Second-hand. Cohort sizes differ by source: 45,750 here, 50,053 for the 27-year follow-up of the same cohort in Table 1, and 50,465 in Hall & Degenhardt (2009), who give 2.4 times for having tried cannabis by 18 (card sc_hall_2009); take the denominator and the exposure contrast from the primary paper.

key_findings.finding: Longitudinal studies: nine of twelve prospective studies reported a significant association of cannabis use with psychotic symptoms or psychotic illness, and the other three a non-significant trend in the same direction (refs 52–64). Table 1 lists 13 adjusted odds ratios (95% CI) with country, design, size and follow-up: Tien & Anthony (USA, 4,494, 1 year) 2.4 (1.2–7.1); Zammit et al. (Swedish conscripts, 50,053, 27 years) 3.1 (1.7–5.5) and Manrique-Garcia et al. (35 years) 1.8 (1.3–2.3); van Os et al. (Netherlands, 4,045, 3 years) 2.8 (1.2–6.5); Weiser et al. (Israel, 9,724, 4–15 years) 2.0 (1.3–3.1); Fergusson et al. (New Zealand, 1,265, 3 years) 1.8 (1.2–2.6); Arseneault et al. (New Zealand, 1,034, 15 years) 4.5 (1.1–18.2); Ferdinand et al. (Netherlands, 1,580, 14 years) 2.8 (1.79–4.43); Henquet et al. (Germany, 2,437, 4 years) 1.7 (1.1–1.5 as printed); Wiles et al. (UK, 8,580, 1.5 years) 1.5 (0.55–3.94); Rössler et al. (Switzerland, 591, 30 years) 1.8 (0.96–3.2); Gage et al. (UK, 1,756, 2 years) 1.1 (0.76–1.65); Rognli et al. (Swedish cohort of discharged prisoners, 6,217, 5 years) 2.6 (1.40–5.0).
key_findings.note: The table gives no exposure contrast, outcome or adjustment set for any estimate, and the count of twelve studies treats the two Swedish conscript reports as one. The Henquet interval excludes its own estimate (reporting issue 1). The odds ratios at the most-exposed level in Marconi et al. (2016) are unadjusted and differ from these (card sc_marconi_2016).

key_findings.finding: Dose–response: a meta-analysis (ref 65, Marconi et al., 2016) is described as showing that the more extensive the use, the greater the risk of psychosis, in all of the studies included, with an odds ratio of almost four for psychosis-related outcomes in the heaviest use compared with none.
key_findings.note: Di Forti is an author of the meta-analysis. Card sc_marconi_2016: pooled odds ratio 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34) at the most-exposed rank, from unadjusted data, I2 82%; category-level odds ratios do not rise steadily in several studies, so in all of the studies overstates.

key_findings.finding: Potency and psychosis: in a south London case–control study of 410 patients with a first episode of psychotic disorder and 390 healthy controls, people who used high-potency cannabis daily were five times more likely than people who had never used to have a psychotic disorder; use of hashish was not associated with increased risk, possibly because of its lower THC and its cannabidiol content (refs 66–68).
key_findings.note: The authors' own study. Card sc_di_forti_2015 gives 410 patients and 370 controls analysed (389 recruited) and an adjusted odds ratio of 5.40 for daily use of skunk-like cannabis; take the numbers from that card.

key_findings.finding: Cannabidiol and psychotic experiences, as cited: in a Dutch survey of 2,000 people who use cannabis, those who preferred cannabis with the highest cannabidiol content had had fewer psychotic-like experiences (ref 69); people whose hair contained both THC and cannabidiol had fewer psychotic symptoms than those with THC only (ref 70); in an experiment with 48 healthy volunteers, oral cannabidiol given before intravenous THC significantly reduced psychotic symptoms (ref 35, Englund et al., 2013).
key_findings.note: The experiment is by a co-author of this review (Englund); the survey and hair-analysis studies are cross-sectional.

key_findings.finding: Case reports of psychosis after very high-THC products such as wax dabs have begun to appear (ref 71), and psychiatric symptoms after synthetic cannabinoids are increasingly reported (ref 72); a systematic overview reported agitation, anxiety, paranoia and psychosis (ref 73), and mounting evidence is said to suggest more chronic psychotic disorders in people who use synthetic cannabinoids persistently (ref 74).

The authors call a cannabis psychosis distinct from schizophrenia dubious: sudden high consumption can cause acute intoxication that usually resolves quickly, which they say is not uncommon with edibles; brief use of plant or synthetic cannabinoids may bring on an acute psychosis that resolves within days or weeks; the longer use goes on, the more the illness comes to resemble schizophrenia (refs 54, 64).

Age at onset: patients with psychosis who used cannabis have a significantly earlier onset than those who never used it (ref 75, a meta-analysis); in one study, daily use of high-potency cannabis went with a first episode of psychosis on average 6 years earlier than in people who had never used (ref 68, Di Forti et al., 2014).

Patients with psychosis who used cannabis tend to score higher on IQ and neurocognitive tests (refs 76, 77), to have had higher premorbid IQ and better premorbid social functioning (ref 78) and to show fewer neurological soft signs (ref 79) than patients who never used; the authors explain this by less neurodevelopmental impairment, describing those who used as often "initially clever and sociable" (no citation for the explanation).
key_findings.note: The explanation is the authors' hypothesis.

key_findings.finding: Criticisms answered: most European and Australasian experts are said to be convinced that cannabis is one of several contributory causes of schizophrenia (no citation), while three sceptical articles have appeared from North America (refs 80–82). Prior vulnerability: the Dunedin study adjusted for psychotic symptoms at 11 and the association remained (ref 58). Self-medication: there is little evidence; in the Christchurch cohort people tended to use less once minor psychotic symptoms developed (ref 83), and patients give the same hedonic reasons for use as others (ref 84). Other drugs: studies that addressed them, including tobacco, did not find them sufficient to negate the effect of cannabis (refs 58, 66, 67). Incidence trends: reliable information is scarce; what the authors call the only competent study spanning decades with the same criteria found that schizophrenia incidence doubled between 1965 and 1999 in south-east London and that the proportion of patients using cannabis rose disproportionately (ref 85, Boydell et al., 2006).
key_findings.locator: CRITICISMS OF THE CAUSAL HYPOTHESIS, 1st–5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: No study reporting stable incidence is cited, although such a study was cited in earlier reviews (Degenhardt, Hall & Lynskey, 2003; card sc_hall_2009). Table 1 includes a cohort whose title reports that psychotic symptoms also predict later cannabis use (ref 59, Ferdinand et al., 2005); that direction is not discussed.

key_findings.finding: Genetic explanations: shared genetic vulnerability is a popular explanation (refs 80, 81, 86); relatives of patients with cannabis-associated psychosis are often psychotic too, but often also use cannabis (ref 87). The polygenic risk score for schizophrenia accounted for only a very small proportion of cannabis use in a large Australian sample (ref 88, Power et al., 2014); a suggestion that people using high-potency cannabis are especially genetically predisposed (ref 89) found no support, according to the review, when the authors examined schizophrenia polygenic scores in people using low- and high-potency cannabis (ref 90, the authors' correspondence reply; no sample size or figures given). No study had yet tested an interaction between the polygenic score and cannabis use; patients with schizophrenia carrying large rare deletions were less likely to have had lifetime cannabis abuse, read as support for a threshold model (ref 91). The COMT moderation reported in Dunedin (ref 92) has had inconsistent replications, and an experiment found no COMT effect on THC-induced psychotic symptoms but a larger working-memory decrement in val/val carriers (ref 93); an AKT1 variant raised psychosis risk among people who use cannabis in two case–control studies and a third found a greater psychotogenic response to smoked cannabis in carriers (refs 94–96), and a DRD2 variant may add to the risk (ref 97).
key_findings.locator: GENETIC PREDISPOSITION OR GENE X ENVIRONMENT INTERACTION?, 1st–5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Power et al. (2014) found that genetic liability to schizophrenia predicts cannabis use, the shared-liability direction; the review reports only that the proportion explained was small. Later Mendelian randomization found stronger evidence from liability to schizophrenia to cannabis use than the reverse (card sc_pasman_2018).

key_findings.finding: Mechanism: patients with psychosis who use cannabis appear more sensitive to its positive and negative effects (ref 84), as do people at high clinical risk (ref 98), and people with schizophrenia reacted more strongly to intravenous THC than controls (ref 24). Human PET evidence on THC-induced dopamine release is equivocal: one study found an increase, another no significant effect, and a re-analysis combining them a small but significant increase (ref 99). People who use cannabis regularly have a low capacity to synthesize and release striatal dopamine but, unlike people dependent on other drugs, no change in striatal D2/D3 receptors (ref 100); the authors propose post-synaptic dopamine supersensitivity (ref 101), as found in animals given chronic THC (ref 102).
key_findings.locator: WHAT IS THE MECHANISM OF ACTION?, 1st–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Connor et al. (2021) describe the same PET source (Bossong et al., 2015) as two small studies with significant increases (card sc_connor_2021).

key_findings.finding: Course and treatment: a meta-analysis found that patients with psychosis who continued using cannabis had higher relapse rates, longer admissions and more severe positive symptoms than those who stopped or never used (ref 103, Schoeler et al., 2016). Cognitive behaviour therapy and motivational interviewing have been tried without great success, tokens for cannabis-free urine tests were under trial, and in a double-blind trial clozapine reduced craving for cannabis, the only pharmacological treatment the authors say has had any success (ref 104).

Dependence: withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, craving, irritability, insomnia, appetite disturbance, dysphoria, depression) are described as generally mild, which the authors attribute, without a citation, to cannabis staying in the body for weeks. Almost 10% of people who use become dependent (refs 105, 106), and some claim 17% if use starts in adolescence (ref 107, Anthony, 2006, a book chapter); dependence is an increasingly common reason for seeking help in Australia, the UK, continental Europe and North America (refs 23, 108), and an internet survey associated high-potency use with an especially increased likelihood of dependence (ref 109, Freeman & Winstock, 2015).
key_findings.locator: OTHER PSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS › Cannabis dependence, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Second-hand. The almost 10% matches the 8.9% lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence in NESARC (ref 106; card sc_lopez_quintero_2011); the 17% traces to the chapter that Hall & Degenhardt (2009) cite for one in six (card sc_hall_2009). The explanation of mild withdrawal is uncited; Connor et al. (2021) report clinically severe withdrawal in 54% of outpatients and 87% of inpatients with CUD seeking treatment (card sc_connor_2021).

key_findings.finding: Other psychiatric disorders: cross-sectional studies show a high prevalence of depression and anxiety disorders in people who use cannabis, but the direction is unclear (refs 110–116); the Swedish conscript cohort showed no increased risk of depression (ref 117); systematic reviews give only weak evidence for affective outcomes (refs 118, 119), though one found a modestly increased risk of depression, slightly stronger with heavy use (ref 120); a large US prospective study found more alcohol, nicotine and other drug use but no more mood or anxiety disorders (ref 121, Blanco et al., 2016). Evidence on PTSD is uncertain; prospective studies are said to show that cannabis use increases the risk of adult ADHD (ref 128). The authors conclude that the evidence of harm is far weaker for depression, anxiety disorders, PTSD and ADHD than for psychosis, and that benefit in PTSD and ADHD remains possible but unproven.
key_findings.locator: OTHER PSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS › Depression and anxiety disorders, 1st–3rd paragraphs; Post-traumatic stress disorder, 1st–2nd paragraphs; Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, 1st paragraph; Summary

key_findings.finding: Brain structure: many studies are small, with inadequate control groups and incomplete control for alcohol (ref 131); two large recent studies found no overall effect of cannabis on brain structure (refs 132, 133), one of them an interaction in which people with a high polygenic risk score for schizophrenia who used cannabis had decreased cortical thickness (ref 132). Potency is rarely considered: high-potency use went with hippocampal volume decrements while cannabidiol-containing preparations did not (ref 134), higher hair cannabidiol with less right hippocampal volume decrement (ref 135), and high-potency use, but not hashish, with disturbed corpus callosum connections (ref 136).
key_findings.locator: EFFECTS ON BRAIN AND COGNITION, 1st–3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Ref 136 has Di Forti among its authors.

key_findings.finding: Cognition: people who use cannabis do worse than people who do not on tests of executive function, attention, verbal ability and memory (refs 137, 138). In the Dunedin cohort, IQ fell by six points between ages 13 and 38 in members repeatedly diagnosed with cannabis use disorder (ref 139, Meier et al., 2012), but shorter studies have failed to replicate this (refs 140, 141: Mokrysz et al., 2016; Jackson et al., 2016). In CARDIA, 5,115 young men and women followed for 25 years, past exposure was associated with worse verbal memory but not with executive function or processing speed (ref 142). Case–control studies usually show worse verbal learning, memory and attention in people who use regularly, more so with longer and more frequent use (ref 143, which the review quotes from Hall & Lynskey, 2016); some studies suggest full recovery after stopping (ref 144), others only partial recovery (ref 142). In a naturalistic study of 134 people, those using cannabis higher in cannabidiol showed no cognitive impairment (ref 145), and among 120 people those whose hair contained both cannabidiol and THC performed better on memory than those with THC only (ref 146).
key_findings.locator: EFFECTS ON BRAIN AND COGNITION, 4th–6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Card sc_meier_2012: about 6 IQ points (−0.38 SD) in the 38 people with 3 or more waves of dependence, with childhood IQ measured at 7–13; about 8 points in the 23 of them with adolescent onset (the figure Hall, 2015, reports). The two non-replications and the recovery evidence contradict the abstract's statement that there are no doubts about detrimental cognitive effects.

key_findings.finding: Adolescent onset: some imaging studies found greater brain changes with adolescent than with adult onset of heavy use, which the authors say await confirmation (ref 138); first use before 17 was associated with lower verbal IQ in people with long-term heavy use (ref 147, Pope et al., 2003); IQ decline was greater in Dunedin members who started in adolescence (cited to ref 148), but social decline was not associated with age at onset (ref 149). Daily use before 17 was associated with clear reductions in completing high school and obtaining a degree in 2,500 young people in Australasia (ref 150, Silins et al., 2014, an integrative analysis by its title), and in a 1-year follow-up of 1,155 adolescents weekly use was related to poorer mathematics and English results (ref 151). In the Dunedin psychosis report, onset at 18 or later carried a small non-significant increase in schizophrenia-like psychosis by 26 and onset at 15 or earlier a fourfold risk (ref 58). The authors suggest that exposure of the developing brain may permanently impair the endocannabinoid system (ref 138).
key_findings.note: Ref 148 is, by its title, a longitudinal study of upper-middle-class youth, not the Dunedin cohort (reporting issue 3); the Dunedin adolescent-onset finding is in Meier et al. (2012), ref 139. For psychosis, the systematic review of Moore et al. (2007) found no robust evidence that earlier first use is more harmful once cumulative use is considered (card sc_moore_2007).

key_findings.finding: Therapeutic use: a German trial found cannabidiol to have antipsychotic effects equivalent to amisulpride in schizophrenia (ref 152), and adding cannabidiol rather than placebo improved psychosis scores in patients partly responding to antipsychotics (ref 153, a conference presentation); smoked THC relieved HIV-associated neuropathic pain (ref 154); inhaled cannabis gave short-term relief of chronic neuropathic pain with a number needed to treat of 5.6 (ref 155); THC or nabiximols can help pain or painful spasms in multiple sclerosis (refs 156, 157); and data on cannabidiol in epilepsy were insufficient for definitive evidence (refs 158–162).
key_findings.locator: THERAPEUTIC USE OF CANNABIS AND ITS COMPONENTS, 2nd–4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Ref 153 was an unpublished conference presentation at the time.

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: with no good animal model of psychosis, conclusive proof of any environmental cause is hard to obtain, and the authors question whether absolute proof should be awaited; they quote the conclusion of Gage et al. (2016) that epidemiological studies justify a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk of psychotic disorders. They acknowledge uncertainty about whether cannabis can induce psychosis without genetic vulnerability, about the proportion of psychosis that would be prevented if nobody used cannabis (estimates of 8–24%, ref 66) and about effects on the brain; they warn against overstating knowledge and against confusing public education with the legalization debate, and note that early reports on legalization and consumption are contradictory (refs 165, 166).
key_findings.note: The 8–24% is cited to the authors' own study; card sc_di_forti_2015 gives attributable fractions of 16.0% to 24.0% in that study and earlier fractions of 6.2% to 14.2% from other cohorts, all assuming causality.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives Henquet et al. (ref 60) an odds ratio of 1.7 with a 95% CI of 1.1–1.5, an interval that excludes its own point estimate.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, PSYCHOSIS › Table 1, Henquet row
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one number is misprinted; take the estimate from the primary paper (Henquet et al., 2005).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives no exposure contrast, outcome definition or adjustment set for any of its 13 estimates although its header calls them adjusted; the Manrique-Garcia row has no country, design or sample size; and the text's twelve studies count the two Swedish conscript reports (Zammit et al.; Manrique-Garcia et al.) as one.
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimates are not comparable with each other and cannot be cited from this table as a set; each must be taken from its primary study with its definitions.

reporting_issues.issue: The greater IQ decline in Dunedin members who started in adolescence is cited to ref 148, whose title describes a longitudinal study of upper-middle-class youth; the Dunedin finding is in ref 139 (Meier et al., 2012).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, ARE ADOLESCENTS ESPECIALLY VULNERABLE?, 2nd paragraph; references 139 and 148
reporting_issues.consequence: Citation error; anchor the claim to Meier et al. (2012).

reporting_issues.issue: The south London case–control study is described as 410 patients and 390 healthy controls; card sc_di_forti_2015 records 410 patients and 370 controls analysed, from 389 controls recruited.
reporting_issues.consequence: Second-hand sample size differs from the primary paper as read in this project; use the primary.

reporting_issues.issue: The Swedish conscript cohort is described as 45,750 men (Andréasson et al., 1987), while Table 1 gives 50,053 for its 27-year follow-up and Hall & Degenhardt (2009) give 50,465 (card sc_hall_2009).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator depends on the report and analysis; take it from the primary paper being cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The meta-analysis of Marconi et al. (2016) is said to show greater risk with more extensive use in all of the studies included; card sc_marconi_2016 records unadjusted data and category-level odds ratios that do not rise steadily in several studies. The review does not say the estimate is unadjusted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Overstatement of consistency; cite the pooled estimate from the meta-analysis with its crude status and heterogeneity (I2 82%).

reporting_issues.issue: The proportion of psychosis preventable if nobody used cannabis is given as 8–24%, cited only to the authors' own study (ref 66); card sc_di_forti_2015 records fractions of 16.0–24.0% in that study and earlier fractions of 6.2%, 8%, 13.3% and 14.2% cited by it, so the range omits the lowest. The review also presents the range as the share of psychosis that could be prevented if nobody used cannabis, without stating that such fractions assume causality, whereas Di Forti et al. (2019, Research in context) describe the 2015 study's 24% as the share of new cases attributable to high-potency cannabis, assuming causality.
reporting_issues.consequence: The range is a selection; attributable fractions should be cited from each primary study, stating that they assume causality.

reporting_issues.issue: The same paper (Gage, Hickman & Zammit, 2016) appears twice in the reference list, as refs 50 and 163.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor duplicate; no effect on content.

reporting_issues.issue: Several statements carry no citation: that most European and Australasian experts are convinced of a contributory cause; that withdrawal is usually mild because cannabis stays in the body for weeks; resin oil of up to 80% THC; and the onset and duration of effects by route.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, CRITICISMS OF THE CAUSAL HYPOTHESIS, 1st paragraph; OTHER PSYCHIATRIC DISORDERS › Cannabis dependence, 1st paragraph; THE CHANGING NATURE OF RECREATIONAL CANNABINOIDS, 3rd paragraph; CANNABINOIDS AND THE ENDOCANNABINOID SYSTEM, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: These cannot be anchored to evidence through this review.

disagreements.first_pass: Genetic explanations: shared genetic vulnerability is a popular explanation (refs 80, 81, 86); relatives of patients with cannabis-associated psychosis are often psychotic too, but often also use cannabis (ref 87). The polygenic risk score for schizophrenia accounted for only a very small proportion of cannabis use in a large Australian sample (ref 88, Power et al., 2014); a suggestion that people using high-potency cannabis are especially genetically predisposed (ref 89) was not supported when their polygenic scores were compared with those of people using low-potency cannabis (ref 90, the authors' reply). No study had yet tested an interaction between the polygenic score and cannabis use; patients with schizophrenia carrying large rare deletions were less likely to have had lifetime cannabis abuse, read as support for a threshold model (ref 91). The COMT moderation reported in Dunedin (ref 92) has had inconsistent replications, and an experiment found no COMT effect on THC-induced psychotic symptoms but a larger working-memory decrement in val/val carriers (ref 93); an AKT1 variant raised psychosis risk among people who use cannabis in two case–control studies and a third found a greater psychotogenic response to smoked cannabis in carriers (refs 94–96), and a DRD2 variant may add to the risk (ref 97).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 216 (second reader): ref 90 is a correspondence reply; the review gives no sample size or figures and says only that no evidence supported greater predisposition.
disagreements.resolution: Checked in the saved PMC text (Genetic predisposition, 2nd paragraph): the review says the authors found no evidence to support the view. Reworded.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract names high-potency cannabis and synthetic cannabinoids as the riskiest forms, a claim that rests on one group's case–control and onset studies of potency (refs 66–68), case reports and a systematic overview of psychopathology after synthetic cannabinoids. It says there are "no such doubts concerning its detrimental effect on cognitive function" (Abstract), while the body reports two failures to replicate the Dunedin IQ decline, full recovery after stopping in some studies, and small, poorly controlled imaging studies. It says all of the negative aspects are magnified when use starts in early adolescence, while the body says the imaging reports await confirmation and that social decline was not associated with age at onset. The conclusion that the evidence for cannabis as a component cause of psychosis suffices for public-health messages is the authors' judgment, supported by a quotation from Gage et al. (2016); the body concedes uncertainty about causation without genetic vulnerability and about the preventable fraction (8–24%, from the authors' own study, assuming causality). The statement that most European and Australasian experts are convinced of a contributory cause carries no citation.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 216 (second reader): wording correction; the review states no causal assumption for the 8–24%.
disagreements.resolution: Checked in the saved PMC text: true. Factual wording corrected; the gap rating (substantial) is unchanged.
